content: “I saw in the night visions, and behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds, and he came to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him near before him. {{v:14}} Dominion was given him, with glory and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.

facets.text: Daniel beholds "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven and approaching the Ancient of Days, from whom he receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom. The heavenly setting and the manner of coming — on the clouds, a divine prerogative — signal that this figure transcends mere humanity even as he appears in human likeness. This vision unveils a mysterious personage who stands before God yet is exalted to share in God's own sovereignty.
facets.question: Who is the mysterious "son of man" who comes on the clouds in Daniel's vision?

facets.text: The dominion given to the son of man is universal, embracing "all the peoples, nations, and languages," and it is everlasting, never to pass away or be destroyed. Unlike the four beastly empires of the surrounding vision, whose power is temporary and violent, this kingdom is imperishable and rightly ordered toward the worship and service of its king. Scripture here proclaims a reign that outlasts every human empire.
facets.question: What makes the kingdom of the son of man different from earthly empires?

facets.text: Catholic tradition reads this vision as a direct prophecy of Jesus Christ, who repeatedly took "Son of Man" as his chosen self-designation and, before Caiaphas, applied Daniel's words to himself as the one who would come on the clouds of heaven. The bestowal of an everlasting kingdom upon the son of man is fulfilled in Christ's resurrection, ascension, and enthronement at the Father's right hand. The Ancient of Days handing over dominion foreshadows the Father glorifying the Son.
facets.question: How does the Church see this vision fulfilled in Jesus Christ?

facets.text: That "all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" reveals a service due to the son of man that Scripture ordinarily reserves for God alone, implying his divine dignity. The worship and everlasting obedience of all nations point beyond a merely political ruler to one who is worthy of adoration, harmonizing with the Church's confession of Christ as true God and true man. The vision thus grounds both the universality of Christ's kingship and the missionary summons to draw all nations to him.
facets.question: Why is the son of man worthy of the service owed to God, and what does this mean for all nations?

facets.text: The vision offers enduring hope to the persecuted People of God: though earthly powers rage like beasts, the final and definitive dominion belongs to the son of man and, through him, to the saints. Because his kingdom "will not be destroyed," the faithful can persevere in confidence that history's last word is God's victory, not the triumph of oppressive powers. This eschatological assurance anchors Christian hope in the coming Kingdom.
facets.question: What hope does this vision offer to God's people suffering under hostile earthly powers?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Daniel's night vision of the "son of man" coming on the clouds to receive an everlasting, universal kingdom from the Ancient of Days; read by the Church as a prophecy of Christ's divine kingship, enthronement, and final victory.

[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: A heavenly figure "like a son of man" comes on the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, appearing in human likeness yet transcending mere humanity.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The son of man's kingdom is universal over all peoples and everlasting, contrasted with the temporary, violent beastly empires of the surrounding vision.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Tradition identifies the son of man as Jesus, who claimed the title and applied Daniel's coming-on-the-clouds to himself; fulfilled in his resurrection, ascension, and enthronement by the Father.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The service of all nations, owed to God alone, implies the son of man's divine dignity, grounding Christ's universal kingship and the mission to all nations.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: The everlasting, indestructible kingdom gives persecuted believers hope that God's victory, not oppressive powers, is history's final word.
